overview.text: The Randolph Urban Renewal Project (Va. R-58) is a Title I redevelopment and conservation effort covering approximately 380 acres in a predominantly Black, lower-income neighborhood of Richmond, Virginia, where 1,117 residential and 58 non-residential buildings will be cleared and over 1,000 others rehabilitated. The community of about 9,000 residents (98% Black) faces high poverty rates yet has stable, long-term residency. Three alternatives were considered—no action, reducing the type/size of the project, or relocating it elsewhere—all rejected as ineffective at eliminating blight. Adverse impacts include construction-related dust, noise, and traffic disruption, relocation of approximately 1,814 families, and air and noise pollution from the adjacent Downtown Expressway, partially mitigated by berms, acoustically treated windows, and air-quality monitoring. Citizen participation through the Randolph Planning Study Board was extensive, residents voted to accept the Plan in November 1972, and most reviewing agencies endorsed the project.

project_description.text: The Randolph Urban Renewal Project (Va. R-58) is a Title I redevelopment and conservation effort covering approximately 380 acres in Richmond, Virginia, divided into redevelopment, rehabilitation, and mixed sub-areas. Of 2,290 principal structures, 1,117 residential buildings (1,613 dwelling units) and 58 non-residential buildings will be cleared, while others will be rehabilitated, maintaining approximate existing residential density. The eight-year program, with gross project cost of approximately $34.6 million, includes new HUD-FHA subsidized housing, separate sanitary/storm sewers, water and gas main modifications, underground utilities in redevelopment areas, and reconstruction/extension of Harrison Street.

affected_community.text: The Randolph Community is a predominantly Black neighborhood of about 9,000 residents (98% Black) in Richmond's West End, bordered by Byrd Park, Hollywood Cemetery, and Riverview Cemetery. The neighborhood is lower-income, with a 1969 mean family income of $7,226 and 22% of families at or below poverty level, and in census tract 413 mean family income was $5,939 versus $10,620 citywide. It comprises 1,086 homeowners, 1,679 renters, and 183 roomers, and despite being mostly renters has long and stable residential roots. There are no health clinics or library within the community, though four schools serve the area.

alternatives_overview.text: Three alternatives were considered: no action, reducing the type and size of the project (e.g., eliminating rehabilitation areas), and relocating the project to another site. All were rejected because they would fail to eliminate blight and would undermine citizen participation. Within the chosen plan, detailed alternatives included closing streets and revising the grid to route through-traffic around the community, extending a street through unused cemetery land, and providing scattered-site public housing in small clusters rather than large complexes.

Relocation of the project would defeat any attempts to eliminate the blight and blighting influences in Randolph.
A continuation of the "no action" policy can therefore be expected to result in considerable citizen reaction.
Detailed planning proposed closing some streets, changing the current grid system for streets, and revising traffic patterns to route heavy traffic around rather than through the community.
The proposal was to extend a street through the vacant cemetery land to connect to another street to allow non-community traffic to by-pass the community.
To provide public housing opportunities throughout the community in small clusters, scattered sites or leased housing, rather than one or two large housing complexes in the area.

environmental_impact.text: Beneficial impacts include replacement of blight and substandard housing, elimination of environmental deficiencies, and improved infrastructure. Adverse short-term impacts include construction-related dust, noise, and traffic disruption, plus relocation of approximately 1,814 families and 49 businesses. The largest adverse impact stems from the adjacent Downtown Expressway, which will increase air and noise pollution, contributing roughly 5,176.6 kg/day of carbon monoxide; existing suspended particulate levels (88 ug/m³ quarterly geometric mean) already exceed the National Ambient Air Quality Standard of 75 ug/m³. Mitigation measures include 15-foot landscaped berms/walls, acoustically treated windows and doors, and ongoing air-quality monitoring; the State Water Control Board found no additional water pollution problems would result if separate sanitary and storm sewers are provided, and noise analyses found all sampled locations to be Normally Acceptable.

public_response.text: Citizen participation was extensive through the Randolph Planning Study Board (RPSB), which worked with the Richmond Redevelopment and Housing Authority over 24 months, after early opposition tied to the planned Downtown Expressway. At a public meeting on November 19, 1972, residents voted to accept the Plan, and the Regional Planning Commission unanimously approved it, congratulating RPSB on citizen participation. The Virginia State Health Department, Richmond City Council, and most reviewing agencies endorsed the project, while EPA expressed no objection but requested more air-quality analysis, and the Federal Highway Administration objected that the EIS overemphasized adverse impacts of the Downtown Expressway.
